newsitem.title: USA: Taiwan committed to China reunification - official.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan committed to China reunification - official.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister, John Chang, told a meeting of southern California's business and political leaders on Monday his island state was committed to reunification with mainland China, but that it would take time.

"It takes time, wisdom, patience, and most important of all, world support, to persuade mainland China to take us as her equal ... there is no easy walk to reunification," Chang told the Los Angeles World Affairs Council, a civic group made up of prominent leaders in commerce and politics.
Chang, coming off successful tours of Europe and Africa, said Taiwan was "committed to China's ... unification."

Mainland China, known as the People's Republic of China, split with Taiwan, which calls itself the Chinese Republic, in 1949. Ever since, the two have been bitter enemies, with China recently holding naval exercises close to Taiwan and condemning Chang's visit to Europe.
Chang stressed that his European trip was "private" as was his appearance in Los Angeles on Monday. As such he was not scheduled to meet with any U.S. government officials.

But he said his message while in the United States was to aid the unification process while pointing out that Taiwan was an important trade partner of the United States and was taking major steps to decrease the trade deficit between the two.
On trade, Chang pointed out that in 1987 the United States had a $16 billion deficit trade balance with Taiwan which had been reduced to $6.8 billion by 1996.
In contrast, America's trade deficit with mainland China had gone from $10.3 billion to $39.5 billion in the same period, Chang said.

In addition to emphasizing the economic benefits of American-Taiwanese trade, Chang called on Washington to aid in the reunification process, while admitting there were "differences and distinctiveness between the Chinese Republic of Taiwan and the Chinese mainland."

However, Chang said, "The reunification of China remains our national policy," but indicated it could only come about when mainland China embraces democracy, a condition Taiwan has voiced on numerous occasions.
